doc.title: Tom Malone interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 3, 2023

title: Atlantic Records fortieth anniversary and the Letterman Sam Ash stunt
summary: Writing Mack the Knife and horn parts for Led Zeppelin night at the Atlantic 40th, then the Letterman show finding a girl at Sam Ash to sit in.

bands.name: Late Show with David Letterman Band

blocks.x: Yeah. They changed all the — you know the writers changed all the original lyrics to funny lyrics. And she was delightful. So you never know. I was an arranger for a show called, a TV special called “The Fortieth Anniversary of Atlantic Records.” It was at the Garden, Madison Square Garden. Giant audience. And it was a 14-1/2 hour concert. It started at 10 in the morning and went ‘til 2:30 in the morning. The closing act was Led Zeppelin, who had not performed for six years. Anyway, everybody in the history of Atlantic Records was there. I had done thirty arrangements before the show, and so we got there and we played with the first act at 10:00, went back to the dressing room and then Ahmet Ertegun comes in the dressing room and he says, “No concert of Atlantic Records would be complete without Bobby Darin being represented.” So I said, “Mack the Knife?” Tim from the Manhattan Transfer is sitting next to me and he says, “I know the song.” So I had brought score paper with me. This was before computers. I started filling out the score, I started writing the chart. And they called my copyist to come in and copy the part. And we walked on stage and sight read the song and he sang the song just bang, just like that. I walked down the hall and I ran into Trevor Rabin. “You guys on the show?” “Yeah.” “What song you doing?” “Owner of the Lonely Heart.” I said, “Wouldn’t it be great if you had real horns playing the horn licks in the middle of the song?” He said, “Yeah can we do that?” You know I knew the parts. You know I had played and recorded with James Brown so I mean those were lifted right out of one of his records. So I wrote out the parts and the horn section went on and sight read them on live TV. The horn section was Alan Rubin, Lou Marini, Tom Scott, and myself. So boom. So I wrote two arrangements after the show started. Another time, the Letterman show, they sent a camera down to 48th Street and they go in with a remote camera — they go into Sam Ash music — here’s a kid with a trumpet case over his shoulder in the store. And they said, “You want to sit in with the Letterman band?” And the kid looks at the camera and says, “When?” They said, “Right now.” The kid ran away. He ran out of the store onto the street. Then they found another kid in there with a tenor sax over his shoulder. “You want to sit in with the Letterman show?” “When?” “Right now.” The kid ran away,

ran out in the street. So now there’s a girl behind the counter. “Do you play an instrument?” “Yes.” “What do you play?” “Alto sax.” “You want to sit in with the Letterman — do you have your horn with you?” “Yeah it’s right here.” “You want to sit in with the Letterman band?” “When?” “Right now.” “Sure.” So the camera’s following her up Broadway to 52nd Street to the studio and she comes up on the stage and Paul says, “What songs do you know?” She says, “Well I don’t know any songs by ear but if you can write them out for me I can play them.” So, “Okay well ‘Isn’t She Lovely,’ Tom what key should she play it in?” Bang, write her a part. Bang, bang, I wrote her out a part, handed it to her. Just as soon as I handed it to her Paul counts off the song. And we did the whole show like that. What song — the rhythm section in the band knew everything so we just basically — you know I just wrote out songs for her that they knew and that was the whole show.
